=== phase 1.10 Gate A evaluator (offline; no COM, no RF, no hardware) ===
test_gate_a                  21 tests, OK
  11 of the 21 drive a FAILURE mode: a context never heard, an ACK before the
  allowlist, too few samples, a context never acked, a missed deadline, an
  unintended ACK, turnaround outside the 192+/-64 us envelope, sequential
  blocks, a token late sample, a reconfigured radio mid-measurement, and a
  malformed field. An evaluator that cannot fail is not a gate.
  2 of the 21 pin the evaluator against a record the REAL firmware emitted,
  through firmware_cli.exe which compiles src/main.c: every field the evaluator
  reads must be present in the live record, and the evaluator must consume it
  without faulting. That check found the firmware gap below.

firmware gap found by writing those two tests:
  main.c's RX record emitted no reason=, while dual_records.c's formatter does.
  Two RX formatters disagreed and main.c's is the live one, so Gate A could not
  have said WHY an unintended ACK should have been refused -- foreign (another
  network) or cross_pair (our own PAN with the wrong short, the more alarming
  of the two). main.c now emits reason=.

a convention error in my own first draft of these tests:
  they used match='foreign' and match='cross_pair'. Those are REASONS, not
  matches: such a frame classifies as match=none with reason=<that>. The tests
  passed against records the firmware cannot emit. Same class of mistake as the
  hex-string-vs-wire-order test vectors in 1.3, caught this time by checking
  against the live record instead of my own assumption.

offline limit, stated rather than hidden:
  the fixture leaves ack_start_us, rssi and lqi at zero, so the ACK turnaround
  envelope and the RF margin numbers can only be VALIDATED on hardware. What is
  validated offline is that the criteria compute correctly and fail correctly
  when given those values.

full corpus after the change: 503 offline C checks + 21 gate-A tests, 0 failures

=== phase 1.12 does the real firmware answer BOTH tuples? (offline) ===
test_dual_pan_ack_flow       15 tests, OK
  Both contexts bound through real BIND commands against the actual src/main.c
  (via tests/firmware_cli.c), then real frames delivered. The dispatcher, the
  per-context ACK gate and the classifier are exercised in one piece rather
  than in isolation or against a model.
  established:  both tuples answered, 6 of 6 each, interleaved
                every frame attributed to its own context (no misattribution)
                ACK completed, zero deadline misses
                config_generation stable at 2 across the exchange
                STATS: ctx0_rx=4 ctx1_rx=4 cross_pair_reject=1 routing_faults=0
  refused (the half that matters more):
                a cross-pair tuple        -> match=none reason=cross_pair, no ACK
                a foreign PAN             -> match=none reason=foreign,    no ACK
                the OTHER context's trust centre under our own tuple
                                          -> match=ctx0 but NO ACK, refused by
                                             the deep predicate rather than the
                                             classifier: frame ctx == key ctx,
                                             not merely frame ctx == tuple
                a wrong key sequence      -> match=ctx1, no ACK
                an unbound context        -> frame arrives, is not answered
                a refusal costs the other context nothing (ctx1,none,ctx1,ctx0
                                             -> 1,0,1,1)
  NOT established here: no timing, no RF margin. The fixture leaves
  ack_start_us, rssi and lqi at zero; those are Gate A on hardware.

fixture gap found by writing this suite:
  @RX memset the event and never stamped config_generation, which
  gate_events.c does on the real capture path. Every fixture RX record read 0,
  so Gate A's "the radio was not reconfigured mid-measurement" criterion could
  not be exercised offline at all. The fixture now stamps it.

=== phase 1.13 the Gate A driver, flow tested offline ===
test_gate_a_runner           14 tests, OK   (identical in container and VM)
  The whole Gate A sequence driven against the actual src/main.c through a
  two-context fake port: INFO identity pin, clock-room check, phase 1 ACK OFF,
  BIND ctx0 then ctx1, phase 2 collection to the sample floor, STATS, END,
  verdict from the same evaluator that will run on hardware.
  established: both binds open the ACK gate (immediate_ack 0 -> 1) and each
               STATUS names its own context and its own assigned_short
               collection reaches >=30 on BOTH contexts and stops near the
               floor rather than running on (the window is a bound, not a
               target: staying on air longer buys nothing)
               routing_faults=0, config_generation=2, both ctx counters > 0
  the guards bite, verified by mutation:
               a wrong identity      -> stops BEFORE any bind (port.bound empty)
               a wrong wire version  -> same
               insufficient clock room -> stops before configuring the radio
               END is attempted even when the gate fails, so the runtime is
               never left bound with an open ACK gate
  real failures caught: a silent ctx1, and sequential blocks (interleaving)
  deliberately expected to FAIL offline on the turnaround criterion: the
  fixture cannot time an ACK, and a test asserting a pass here would assert a
  lie.

two defects of my own found by running it:
  INFO carries boot. INFO's field set is `id` alone -- it is the handshake that
  reveals boot, so requiring it would be circular -- and the firmware correctly
  refused the second INFO with field_set. The firmware and the contract were
  right; the host was wrong. Fixed host-side, and the host now checks the boot
  in the RESPONSE against what it knows, which is the stronger direction.
  rx_counts() scanned all records while the phase-2 evidence was a later
  slice, so frames arriving during the post-bind INFO exchange counted toward
  the stop condition without being in the evidence. Collection stopped at 29
  of 30 while believing it had reached the floor. Now counted over the same
  slice that becomes the evidence.

=== phase 1.14 the Gate A authority, and a correction to my own design ===
test_gate_a_authority        40 tests, OK (1 skipped where the sealed
                             inventory is absent)
  prior gate: each of the five closure flags required, a prior error refused,
              and the LINEAGE LINK -- ctx1's store today must still be the one
              V25 left. Verified against the committed hardware_result.json:
              final_CURRENT_sha256 9eef08a7722e... is exactly the hash
              dual_store read from the live ctx1 store.
  software:   a failed review, a review that already touched hardware, an
              image the manifest does not describe, an image the review did
              not review, a manifest claiming it was flashed, an image not
              bit-comparable with the lineage, a source that moved since
              review, a firmware input that moved since the build (the check
              that already refused a stale image once here), and one that
              vanished.
  device:     exactly one positively identified dongle or a refusal; two
              matches is a refusal rather than a choice; the right serial on
              the wrong VID is not a match.

the correction, which is the important part:
  My first draft had BOTH stores leave the protected inventory, reasoning that
  ctx0 becomes a live participant in Gate A so its store legitimately moves.
  That is wrong for Gate A. Gate A sends no secured frame: it binds, listens,
  reads counters and ends. No frame counter is spent, no generation advances,
  and nothing on the host writes a store -- dual_store is read-only by
  construction. So the correct expectation is that BOTH stores come out
  byte-unchanged and ctx0 stays sealed exactly as since issue #4.
  I would have shipped a guard permitting a store to move during a gate with
  no business moving it, and the permission would have been invisible because
  nothing would ever have exercised it.
  The relaxation belongs to Gate B, where secured rejoin genuinely advances
  ctx0. transitions() is kept for that gate; Gate A uses a separate, strict
  gate_a_store_expectation(). The two are deliberately apart so loosening the
  general rule cannot silently loosen Gate A -- there is a test asserting that
  a generation rise passes transitions() and fails Gate A.
  GATE_A_PROCEDURE.md section 2 is rewritten to say this, with the first
  version's claim named as wrong rather than quietly replaced.

inventory asymmetry, handled rather than assumed:
  protected_before.json holds only ctx0's store (13 entries), because ctx1's
  belongs to the milestone that owns the inventory and prepare.py skips its own
  directory. There is a test for both halves of that.

operational note: protected_unchanged() over the mounted filesystem from the
Linux VM did not finish inside a 150 s bounded call -- re-hashing 353 files
across the mount. The sealed side is instant, so it is filesystem cost and not
a bug. The guard runs natively on Windows, where this is not a factor.

=== phase 1.15 the Gate A launcher (one-shot; runs on the operator's machine) ===
launch_gate_a.py is deliberately thin: the authority, the sequence and the
evaluation are all tested offline elsewhere, so what is left here is only what
cannot be tested without the real machine -- opening the port, the one-shot
bookkeeping, and writing the outcome.
  --prepare  checks everything checkable without the radio, then mints a run id
             into an immutable milestone.json
  --run ID   re-runs the preflight (the operator flashed in between, and a
             check made before the thing it guards is not a guard), refuses if
             a store moved between prepare and run, selects the one dongle,
             drives the gate, then snapshots both stores and the protected
             inventory AGAIN and records any violation
hardware_pass requires all three: the verdict passed, zero store violations,
zero protected-file changes.
verified offline: a missing artifact is a named refusal with exit code 2, not a
traceback -- the operator reads this on their own machine and needs to know
which artifact is absent; a refused --prepare leaves nothing behind at all; and
.local/ is gitignored, so run artifacts never enter the repository.

=== phase 1.16 review.py — the offline review the Gate A guard pins ===
Runs every offline suite, hashes every reviewed host/test source, pins the
image and its manifest, and REFUSES to write evidence/review.json if anything
failed. The guard refuses to run without a passing review, so the sequence is
review first, hardware second, and hardware_performed=false is recorded and
checked.

first run (--dry-run), in the container:
  native corpus                                    passed
  test_gate_a                                      passed
  test_gate_a_runner                               passed
  test_gate_a_authority                            passed
  test_dual_store                                  passed
  test_dual_pan_ack_flow                           passed
  test_completion test_clock_dispatch
  test_permit_observation test_mac_backoff
  test_peer_scope test_foreign_status_scope
  test_first_control                               all passed
  review NOT written, one failure:
      "firmware sources moved after the build: ['src/main.c']"

That is the correct and only blocker, and review.py found it independently of
my having noted it by hand in 1.10: main.c gained reason= on the RX record
after the lineage image was built, so the image no longer describes the tree.
The release image must be rebuilt with the operator's lineage toolchain before
Gate A, and the review will then seal.

=== phase 1.17 the ACK timing criterion, corrected against the real capture path ===
test_gate_a                  28 tests, OK  (21 before; +7)

provenance checked rather than assumed. The four RX timestamps are hardware
captures from TIMER3, and each was traced to its source:
  time_us        CC[0]  CRCOK    gate_events.c, "not a software read"
  ack_start_us   CC[1]  TXREADY  gate_hw_ack_started
  ack_address_us CC[3]  ADDRESS  gate_hw_ack_started
  ack_end_us     CC[2]  PHYEND   gate_hw_ack_completed
  rssi / lqi              from nrf_802154_received_timestamp_raw, the driver's
                          own RX callback, so the RF margin really is measured
  ack_completed           from irq_phyend_state_tx_ack in the driver -- the
                          PHYEND of the ACK itself, NOT the AR bit. The
                          protocol contract requires exactly that
                          ("ack_sent только по факту завершения ACK, не по
                          AR=1") and the firmware satisfies it.
  deadline_miss           from the driver's else-branch where the ACK could
                          not be started in time.

a weakness in my own evaluator, found by that check:
  it asserted turnaround = CC[1]-CC[0] against 192 +/- 64 us. But TXREADY
  precedes the ACK's air time and ADDRESS follows its preamble, so NEITHER
  capture is exactly "ACK start on air". A tight assertion risked failing the
  gate on a definitional mismatch -- the worst false negative, because it
  sends someone hunting a radio fault that does not exist.
  Replaced by two checks:
    1. ORDERING: CRCOK < TXREADY <= ADDRESS < PHYEND. True whatever the
       reference points mean, and no correct capture path can violate it. A
       mis-wired PPI channel or a CC clash surfaces here instead of silently
       corrupting every number -- which is the exact failure a CC[0] clash
       nearly caused earlier in this project.
    2. A GENEROUS envelope, 32..352 us, plus an ACK-duration plausibility
       bound, with all three distributions reported so the hardware defines
       the tight numbers rather than this file guessing them in advance.
  new tests: TXREADY before CRCOK caught, PHYEND before ADDRESS caught, the
  violation recorded with all four captures, an implausible ACK duration
  caught, and all three timing figures reported.

=== phase 1.18 the review runs where the host toolchain is ===
The first version of review.py ran `sh tests/run_native.sh` and died on
Windows with a traceback, because Windows has neither a POSIX shell nor a host
C compiler. My design error, not the operator's: the ARM build belongs on
Windows because only Windows has the LINEAGE toolchain, but the review needs a
HOST toolchain, and those are two different things that I had conflated into
one script.
  review.py now refuses by name -- "this review needs sh and gcc, which this
  host does not have" -- with exit code 2 and the division of labour stated,
  rather than a traceback. Verified by running it with an empty PATH.
  The Windows build script no longer runs it, and records why in the script
  itself so the omission does not read as forgetfulness.
  Both hosts see the same files through the same folder, so the review seals
  the same image either way.

=== phase 1.19 the protected-inventory check, measured instead of assumed ===
test_gate_a_authority        50 tests, OK (1 skipped)

Two separate problems, both found by running the preflight on a host that was
not the build host rather than by reading the code.

1. sdk_root was not portable. The manifest records it as the build host's
   absolute Windows path. I had made the input hash KEYS repository-relative so
   the evidence travels between hosts, and left sdk_root absolute -- so the
   firmware-input check, roughly 50 SDK files, failed everywhere but Windows.
   Now located the way tools/build.py locates it, three levels above the repo
   root, with the recorded path only a fallback, and a refusal naming both
   paths tried if neither resolves. Silently skipping the SDK inputs would drop
   them out of the very check that refuses an image built before the sources
   moved. 4 new tests.

2. The walk could not finish. prepare.py uses rglob('*') and filters after, so
   it enumerates every file under zig-global before discarding it: two
   milestones hold 1799 such files each. Measured ~330 s over the mount against
   1.8 s to stat the 354 files that matter. A pruning walk in this module does
   the same job in 16 s -- 20x -- and prepare.py, another milestone's frozen
   file, is not edited. The two are proved identical on a synthetic tree built
   for the purpose, including the edge case that a FILE named zig-local is
   excluded too, because prepare.py tests every path component and pruning
   directories alone would miss it. 4 new tests.

Then the real finding, which changed the semantics:
   live inventory 628 files, sealed inventory 354, so a whole-set comparison
   reports 274 differences and the guard refuses. Measured: all 354 sealed
   files present and byte-identical, 0 missing and 0 modified; the 274 are run
   artifacts added by the ctx1_* gates of the V22..V25 lineage AFTER issue #4
   took its snapshot.
   The tempting cure -- excluding milestone prefixes until the comparison
   passes -- weakens the check until it is green, which is the anti-pattern
   this guard exists to prevent. The question is split instead:
     sealed_integrity()      a sealed file missing or modified is a REFUSAL
     additions_since_seal()  reported and accounted for, but every one must
                             sit under some milestone's .local; one anywhere
                             else is STRAY and a refusal
   The strong half stays strict and the benign half stops failing. 8 new tests.

FULL PREFLIGHT ON THE OPERATOR'S MACHINE, no radio: PASSED in 21 s
   image     32395A9F6B9C1FD3093F1E84E6235EBF76B7B462C3C1C3DB80B73D3C73F1B4DB
   protected 628 walked, 354 sealed intact, 274 additions, 0 stray
   ctx0      gen=19 next_fc=1280 epoch=017af4be2e55
   ctx1      gen=16 next_fc=1088 epoch=9eef08a7722e
   prior gate closed; ctx1 store still the one V25 left

Also confirmed twice over: the guard refused with
reviewed_source_changed:gate_a_authority.py each time I edited a reviewed
source after sealing the review. The review-then-hardware order is enforced by
the machinery, not by my memory.
